title: LEFT JOIN
objective: Use LEFT JOIN to keep every row of the driving table, handle the NULLs it produces, write anti-joins, and put right-table filters in ON (not WHERE) so the LEFT JOIN is not silently turned into an INNER JOIN.
context: Customer success needs lists that include the customers who did NOT do something — never ordered, no order this year, no valid order. Those rows are exactly what an INNER JOIN throws away.

exercises.title: Every customer's order count
exercises.question: Customer success wants an order count for EVERY customer, including those who never ordered.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and order_count (orders of any status; 0 when none) for all 20 customers.
hints: 'Every customer' → customers is the driving table and must survive → LEFT JOIN.
COUNT(o.order_id) is 0 for the NULL-padded row; COUNT(*) would say 1.
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
exercises.why: Zero-activity customers are the target list for re-engagement campaigns. An INNER JOIN would hide them.

recall.q: A customer has no orders. What does COUNT(*) give after a LEFT JOIN? COUNT(o.order_id)?

exercises.join_notes: customers 20, orders 60. Before grouping: 62 rows = 59 order rows that match a customer (one-to-many: customer 1 repeats 9 times) + 3 NULL-padded rows for customers 18, 19 and 20, who have no orders. After GROUP BY: 20 rows; those three get order_count 0. The counts add up to 59, not 60: order 31 (customer 99) is not attached to any customer — a LEFT JOIN from customers keeps all customers, not all orders.

exercises.title: Every product with its supplier (or NULL)
exercises.question: Procurement wants the COMPLETE product list with supplier name, flagging gaps instead of hiding them.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and supplier_name for all 25 products (supplier_name NULL when the product has no matching supplier).
hints: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, s.supplier_name FROM products p LEFT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id;
exercises.why: A complete list with visible NULLs is honest; an INNER JOIN list that is silently 2 rows short is not.

recall.q: In a LEFT JOIN, which side's columns can become NULL because of the join?

exercises.join_notes: products 25 → 25 rows (each product matches at most one supplier, so no multiplication). Compare with the INNER JOIN in Lesson 10 (23 rows): the two extra rows are product 21 'Water Bottle' (supplier_id 9 doesn't exist) and product 22 'Phone Stand' (NULL supplier_id), both with supplier_name NULL. Supplier 5 still doesn't appear — LEFT JOIN protects the left table only.

exercises.title: Products that were never sold (anti-join)
exercises.question: Merchandising wants to delist dead stock: which products have never appeared on any order line?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id and product_name of products that appear on no order line at all.
hints: Keep products, look for the ones whose match came back empty.
After the LEFT JOIN, test a right-table column that is never NULL in real rows (its primary key).
FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id WHERE oi.order_item_id IS NULL
exercises.why: 'Which X has no Y?' (no orders, no logins, no payments) is one of the most-asked analytics questions.

recall.q: Why test the right table's primary key for NULL in an anti-join?
recall.a: The PK is never NULL in a real row, so NULL there can only mean 'no match'.

exercises.join_notes: products 25, order_items 150. The LEFT JOIN produces 153 rows: 150 line rows (one-to-many — product 9 alone repeats 15 times) plus 3 NULL-padded rows for products 23 'Smart Watch', 24 'Linen Tablecloth' and 25 'Tennis Racket'. WHERE oi.order_item_id IS NULL keeps exactly those 3.

exercises.title: Orders in 2025 per customer — filter in ON, not WHERE
exercises.question: Customer success: for EVERY customer, how many orders did they place in 2025? Zero is an answer.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and orders_2025 (orders of any status with order_date >= '2025-01-01'; 0 when none) for all 20 customers.
hints: The date filter is about the RIGHT table (orders). Where must it go so customers still survive?
If you write WHERE o.order_date >= ..., customers with no 2025 order get NULL dates and are removed.
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'
exercises.why: This is the most common LEFT JOIN bug in production SQL: a WHERE on the right table quietly converts the LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN and the zero rows disappear from the report.

recall.q: Why does WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' break a LEFT JOIN from customers?
recall.a: Unmatched customers have NULL order_date; NULL >= '2025-01-01' is not true, so WHERE removes them — the LEFT JOIN acts like an INNER JOIN.

exercises.join_notes: With the date filter in ON: 20 rows. Customers 5 and 8 (only 2024 orders) and 18, 19, 20 (no orders at all) still appear, with orders_2025 = 0 — their NULL-padded row is counted as 0 by COUNT(o.order_id). Moving the filter to WHERE returns only 15 rows: those 5 customers are dropped because their o.order_date is NULL (or 2024). The 2025 counts sum to 29, not 30 — order 31 belongs to customer 99 who isn't in customers.

exercises.title: Every order with its line count and value
exercises.question: Operations wants all 60 orders with how many lines and how much value each has — empty orders included.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_status, line_count (number of order lines; 0 when none) and order_value (SUM(quantity * unit_price) rounded to 2 decimals; 0 when the order has no lines) for all 60 orders.
hints: All 60 orders → orders is the left table.
SUM over only NULLs is NULL, not 0 — wrap it in COALESCE(..., 0).
COUNT(oi.order_item_id) AS line_count, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0), 2) AS order_value
exercises.why: Header/detail reports must not lose headers that have no detail yet (pending, draft, empty baskets).

recall.q: What does SUM() return when all inputs are NULL?

exercises.join_notes: orders 60, order_items 150. The LEFT JOIN yields 151 rows: 150 line rows (each order repeated once per line, up to 5 times) + 1 NULL-padded row for order 60 (pending, no items). GROUP BY collapses back to 60 rows. Order 60 shows line_count 0 and order_value 0 — without COALESCE its value would be NULL. An INNER JOIN would have returned only 59 orders.

exercises.title: Last valid order per customer (and days since)
exercises.question: Retention wants each customer's most recent VALID order and how long ago it was, as of 2025-12-31.
exercises.prompt: For all 20 customers return customer_id, name, last_order_date (latest order_date among their valid orders: order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); NULL if none) and days_since_last_order (whole days from last_order_date to '2025-12-31': CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(last_order_date) AS INTEGER); NULL if none).
hints: The status filter is on the right table and all 20 customers must survive → it goes in ON.
MAX(o.order_date) per customer; julianday() turns dates into day numbers you can subtract.
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
exercises.why: Recency is the R in RFM segmentation. Customers with NULL recency are a segment of their own, not an error to hide.

recall.q: Customer 16 has one order, which was cancelled. What does this query show for them, and why?
recall.a: NULL last_order_date: the cancelled order fails the ON condition, so customer 16 gets a NULL-padded row.

exercises.join_notes: 20 customers → 20 rows. 16 customers have at least one valid order. Four come back NULL: customers 18, 19 and 20 have no orders at all, and customer 16 (Ava Thompson) has only order 48, which is cancelled — the status condition in ON rejects it, so she gets a NULL-padded row. Customer 13's pending order 59 is ignored the same way, so their last valid order is 2025-01-15 (350 days). Put the status filter in WHERE and customer 16 plus 18–20 would vanish (16 rows).

worked_example.question: Show every product with how many order lines it appears on (0 if never sold).
worked_example.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       COUNT(oi.order_item_id) AS line_count
FROM products AS p
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY line_count, p.product_id
LIMIT 6;
worked_example.explanation: All 25 products survive. Products 23, 24, 25 have no lines: they appear once with NULL order_item_id, which COUNT(oi.order_item_id) turns into 0. With an INNER JOIN they would be invisible.

recipe:
**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

**LEFT JOIN = all left rows + matching right rows.** If a left row has no match, it appears once with
**NULL in every right-table column**.

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS cancelled_orders          -- count a RIGHT column → 0 for no match
FROM   customers AS c                                 -- every customer must survive
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
       AND o.order_status = 'cancelled'               -- right-table filter goes in ON
GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.name;
-- predict: 20 customers → 20 rows
```

**Filter-in-ON vs filter-in-WHERE (the #1 LEFT JOIN bug)**
- `ON ... AND o.x = ...` → filters which right rows *match*; left rows still survive (with NULLs).
- `WHERE o.x = ...` → runs *after* the join; NULL-padded rows fail the test and are removed →
  your LEFT JOIN has silently become an INNER JOIN.
- Filters on the **left** table belong in WHERE as usual.

**Anti-join:** `LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL` keeps only left rows with *no* match
(same as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM right WHERE …)`).

**NULL handling:** `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` turns 'no rows' into 0; `COUNT(right.col)` already returns 0.
common_mistakes: Filtering the right table in WHERE (`WHERE o.status = ...`) — it removes the NULL-padded rows and turns LEFT into INNER.
Using COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN — unmatched left rows count as 1 instead of 0.
Forgetting COALESCE around SUM — 'no rows' gives NULL, not 0.
Testing a left-table column for NULL in an anti-join instead of the right table's key.
Assuming LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of BOTH tables — it only protects the left one (order 31 still disappears from customers LEFT JOIN orders).
recall: What appears in the right-table columns for an unmatched left row?
Right-table filter: ON or WHERE in a LEFT JOIN?
ON — in WHERE it eliminates the unmatched rows and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN.
FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.key = a.key WHERE b.key IS NULL
Can a LEFT JOIN return more rows than the left table?
Yes — when a left row matches several right rows (one-to-many).
